articles.title: West Hollywood Is Adding New Housing Along Santa Monica Boulevard: What Buyers and Owners Should Watch
articles.body_html:
West Hollywood is in the middle of a visible housing and development cycle, particularly along and near Santa Monica Boulevard. Several projects are moving at once, including a substantial mixed-use building at Santa Monica Boulevard and Crescent Heights and the newly completed Marigold West affordable senior development near the corridor.

For buyers and existing homeowners, that does not automatically mean values are going up or down. What matters is how individual projects change housing supply, streets, retail activity, views, traffic and the experience of living on a particular block.

What is being built at 8025 Santa Monica Boulevard?

One of the most visible current projects is at 8025 Santa Monica Boulevard, at Crescent Heights. The seven-story mixed-use development is now rising above the site, with apartments, ground-floor commercial space and structured parking.

Recent project reporting describes 115 studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom apartments. City approval records have reflected revisions during the entitlement process, so buyers evaluating a nearby property should focus on the current approved and permitted project rather than an old marketing summary.

That intersection matters because it sits along one of West Hollywood's principal commercial corridors and within walking distance of a substantial concentration of restaurants, shops, nightlife and housing. This is the type of project that can gradually change the character of a corridor without transforming an entire neighborhood overnight.

West Hollywood is adding housing in several forms

The larger story is not a single apartment building. On September 10, construction wrapped on Marigold West at 1041 N. Martel Avenue, just south of Santa Monica Boulevard. The five-story project contains 50 affordable studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom homes reserved for residents 62 and older. Half are intended for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness.

Other infill projects are also moving through West Hollywood. The result is not one giant construction wave. It is a series of projects of very different sizes occurring across a relatively small city.

Does new apartment construction affect nearby condo values?

Potentially, but not in a simple way. New rental housing does not necessarily compete directly with an existing condominium. A buyer considering a two-bedroom condo may not view a new luxury apartment as a substitute for ownership. But development can still affect the surrounding market.

Mixed-use projects can add residents and commercial spaces to corridors that previously contained lower-density buildings or underused lots. More residents can support restaurants, grocery stores, fitness businesses and neighborhood services. That can improve daily convenience.

For a condo owner immediately adjacent to new construction, the impact can be different. A new multi-story building may affect views, natural light or privacy. That is why buyers should look beyond the unit itself and consider what could potentially happen on nearby parcels.

Development also brings temporary disruption. Noise, trucks, lane closures and construction activity can make a block less pleasant even when the completed project eventually improves the corridor. Repeated projects can also add meaningfully to the city's housing stock over time.

Why is Santa Monica Boulevard attracting development?

Santa Monica Boulevard already functions as West Hollywood's major east-west commercial spine. It offers a concentration of restaurants, nightlife, retail, services and employment within a city where many residents value being able to walk for at least some daily needs.

That makes sites along the corridor logical locations for denser residential and mixed-use construction. It is also worth remembering that West Hollywood is its own incorporated city. A project in West Hollywood is governed by West Hollywood land-use rules rather than City of Los Angeles zoning, even though traveling a few blocks can put you back inside Los Angeles.

Should buyers be concerned about development near a property?

They should be informed, not automatically concerned. If you are considering buying a condo and there is a one-story commercial building directly across the street, I would not assume that building will stay one story forever.

Look at the surrounding parcels. Ask whether there are active entitlement applications. Look at current construction. Consider whether an adjacent property appears underdeveloped relative to the corridor. None of that means a project will definitely happen. It means the buyer is evaluating the surrounding real estate rather than treating the current view as permanent.

Could more housing improve the neighborhood?

It can. Additional residents create customers for local businesses. New projects may replace vacant, aging or low-intensity commercial properties with buildings that put more people directly on the corridor. Ground-floor commercial space can also introduce new restaurants and services.

But good neighborhood development depends on more than adding units. Architecture, sidewalk design, parking access, landscaping, ground-floor uses and the relationship of the building to surrounding homes all affect whether a project improves the pedestrian experience.

What does this mean for West Hollywood sellers?

For most sellers, the useful approach is explaining the property's actual context rather than making broad claims about redevelopment. Is the condo two blocks from a growing concentration of restaurants? Is a long-vacant site nearby becoming housing? Will a particular development add retail? Could construction temporarily affect access? Does the unit have a protected orientation, or could another building eventually rise nearby?

Those are useful details because they help a buyer understand the property as part of a changing neighborhood.

What should investors watch?

West Hollywood development can provide information about where capital and developers see demand. But investors should not infer that every property near new construction is automatically undervalued. Look at actual rents, vacancy, regulations, acquisition price and operating expenses.

Also distinguish between West Hollywood and the City of Los Angeles because rental regulations differ across municipal boundaries.

Frequently asked questions

What is being built at 8025 Santa Monica Boulevard? A seven-story mixed-use apartment project with ground-floor commercial space is under construction at Santa Monica Boulevard and Crescent Heights.

Is West Hollywood adding affordable housing? Yes. Marigold West recently completed 50 affordable senior apartments near Santa Monica Boulevard.

Does new construction lower existing home values? Not necessarily. Effects can vary based on property type, proximity, views, amenities, noise, streetscape improvements and the quality of the finished development.

Should condo buyers research nearby development? Yes. Understanding active projects and potentially developable neighboring sites is a useful part of neighborhood due diligence.

Paul's take

West Hollywood is already a built-out, highly desirable city, which means change tends to happen parcel by parcel rather than through giant new subdivisions. That makes individual development sites more important.

When I evaluate a West Hollywood property, I want to understand not only what the block looks like today, but what is being built around it and how that could change the experience of owning there.

articles.title: The Lucas Museum Opens September 22: What It Adds to Exposition Park and South Los Angeles
articles.body_html:
One of Los Angeles' biggest cultural openings in years is about to arrive in Exposition Park.

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens to the public Tuesday, September 22, bringing a 300,000-square-foot museum, more than 100,000 square feet of gallery space, a 13-acre landscaped campus and a destination restaurant to an area already home to USC, the California Science Center, Natural History Museum, Memorial Coliseum and BMO Stadium.

For Los Angeles residents, this is more than another place to visit on a weekend. It strengthens Exposition Park as one of the city's major cultural districts.

What exactly is the Lucas Museum?

The museum was founded by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson around the idea of narrative art, essentially the ways humans tell stories through images.

Its collections cross traditional boundaries among fine art, illustration, comics and cinema. The museum says its opening exhibitions will include more than 1,300 works spread across more than 30 galleries. Artists and creators represented range from Norman Rockwell, Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo and Gordon Parks to comic, mural and cinematic artists.

The museum also houses the Lucas Archives, with materials from Lucasfilm productions including Star Wars and Indiana Jones. The broader mission is not limited to film. It treats cinema as one part of a much longer history of visual storytelling.

The building itself is part of the attraction

The museum was designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects with Stantec. Instead of appearing as a conventional rectangular museum, the building rises over parts of the surrounding landscape in a flowing form designed to blend architecture and park.

The museum says its exterior uses more than 1,200 uniquely shaped curved panels. Whether someone loves the design or not, it adds an unmistakable piece of contemporary architecture to Exposition Park.

Los Angeles neighborhoods are shaped by cultural architecture as well as housing. The Getty Center helps define Brentwood, Disney Concert Hall helps define the Civic Center, and Griffith Observatory shapes the identity of Griffith Park. The Lucas Museum has the potential to play a similar role for Exposition Park.

What happened to the land around the museum?

One of the most interesting parts of the project is outside the building. The museum sits within a new 13-acre park and garden designed by Mia Lehrer and Studio-MLA.

According to the museum, the site previously contained asphalt parking. It now includes more than 300 new trees, meadows, an amphitheater, a hanging garden, public sculptures and landscaped gathering areas.

That is meaningful neighborhood infrastructure. The gardens are not simply decoration for museum ticket holders. The museum says the park is free and open to the public.

In a city where shade and public green space can vary dramatically by neighborhood, converting parking into a substantial landscaped campus changes how the site functions even for people who never buy a museum ticket.

What else is opening there?

The project also adds a major new restaurant. Skywalker Grill opens September 22 at the top of the museum.

It will serve lunch, dinner and weekend brunch and will be open to the public, including people who are not visiting museum galleries. The restaurant was designed by Rockwell Group and will feature panoramic views over Los Angeles.

This is one reason cultural institutions can have effects beyond their exhibition halls. They bring visitors who then eat, shop, park, use transit and spend time in surrounding neighborhoods.

Why Exposition Park?

Exposition Park already has an unusual concentration of destinations. USC sits immediately north. The Natural History Museum and California Science Center are nearby. The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum and BMO Stadium bring major sporting events. Metro's E Line provides rail service through the area.

Adding the Lucas Museum strengthens a district that increasingly functions as both a neighborhood amenity and a regional destination.

Does a new museum affect nearby real estate values?

It can contribute to neighborhood desirability, but I would be careful about making a direct value claim.

A major cultural institution can improve visibility, bring investment, add amenities and create reasons for people to visit an area. Those are real neighborhood characteristics.

But a homeowner cannot reasonably say the museum opened, therefore my house is worth a specific percentage more. Real estate values depend on comparable sales, property condition, location, schools, financing conditions, housing supply and many other factors.

The more useful real-estate question is whether an area is gaining amenities and infrastructure that make daily life more compelling over time. Exposition Park clearly is.

What could this mean for people considering nearby neighborhoods?

A buyer considering areas around USC or Exposition Park should think about both benefits and tradeoffs.

Being near museums, sporting venues, USC and rail gives residents access to an unusually large concentration of activities. The same attractions can generate traffic, parking demand and crowds. A quiet weekday morning can feel completely different from a USC football Saturday.

The E Line makes parts of the district accessible without a car and connects the area toward Downtown Los Angeles and the Westside. Large institutions can also attract additional restaurants, housing and commercial investment. Buyers should track projects around the area rather than assuming today's built environment will remain static.

Can you visit the park without entering the museum?

Yes. The museum describes the new park as free and open to the public. That may end up being one of the most important everyday additions for nearby residents. Museums are destinations. Parks can become routines.

What does admission cost?

Current museum information lists general adult admission at $25, $21 for visitors 65 and older, and free admission for children 17 and under. Timed entry reservations are required.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Lucas Museum open? Tuesday, September 22, 2026.

Where is the Lucas Museum? It is in Exposition Park at One Lucas Plaza, 3800 S. Vermont Avenue.

Is the park free? The museum says its surrounding 13-acre park and gardens are free and open to the public.

Does the museum have a restaurant? Yes. Skywalker Grill opens with the museum and is accessible to the general public.

Is it only a Star Wars museum? No. Star Wars materials are part of the collection, but the museum's broader mission covers narrative art across centuries, cultures and mediums.

Paul's take

One of the things I like about following Los Angeles real estate is that neighborhood change is not only about apartment counts and sale prices.

A museum, park, restaurant or transit improvement can change how people actually experience an area. The Lucas Museum adds all of those elements at once: a major cultural institution, new architecture, public green space and dining. That makes its opening worth watching well beyond opening weekend.

articles.title: Los Angeles Just Cause Ordinance: What Owners of Non-RSO Rental Property Need to Know
articles.body_html:
Owning a rental property that is not covered by Los Angeles' Rent Stabilization Ordinance does not necessarily mean the property is free from local tenant protections.

The City of Los Angeles' Just Cause Ordinance, or JCO, covers most residential rental properties in the city that are not subject to the RSO. It regulates when a landlord may terminate certain tenancies and can require relocation assistance for no-fault evictions. LAHD updated its current JCO guidance on September 10, 2026.

For investors, this distinction is important because not RSO and not regulated are not the same thing.

What is the Los Angeles Just Cause Ordinance?

The JCO creates local just-cause protections for many tenants living in rental housing that falls outside the RSO.

LAHD says the ordinance generally applies after the tenant has occupied the same unit for at least six months or after the original lease expires, whichever happens first. Once the protections apply, an owner cannot simply terminate the tenancy without a recognized reason.

There are exceptions, so owners should verify the specific property's status rather than relying on a general description.

Is JCO the same as RSO?

No. This is probably the most important distinction.

The RSO, or Rent Stabilization Ordinance, regulates qualifying older rental properties and includes rules governing allowable rent increases and evictions.

The JCO generally provides just-cause eviction protections to many City of Los Angeles rental units that are not under the RSO. LAHD states directly that JCO can apply to newer buildings and can even apply to a property containing only a single-family home.

That makes the JCO relevant to far more than traditional apartment buildings.

Does JCO control rent increases?

The JCO itself does not regulate rent increases. But that does not necessarily mean an owner can increase rent without another limitation.

State law, including California's Tenant Protection Act commonly associated with AB 1482, can separately regulate annual rent increases for qualifying properties.

The result is that a property can fall into several different regulatory categories. A property might not be covered by the Los Angeles RSO, be covered by the Los Angeles JCO, and also be subject to state rent limitations. Or it may qualify for an exemption from one of those laws.

That is why investors should avoid using non-RSO as shorthand for unregulated.

What are at-fault reasons for eviction?

LAHD's current guidance lists several circumstances that may constitute at-fault just cause.

Examples include failure to pay rent, violating a rental agreement and failing to cure the violation, causing a nuisance or damaging the property, illegal use of the unit, refusing reasonable access, and certain unauthorized subtenant situations.

When an eviction is based on recognized tenant fault, relocation assistance generally is not required under the JCO. An owner considering an actual eviction should consult qualified legal counsel because notice requirements, documentation and facts matter.

What is a no-fault eviction?

A no-fault eviction is based on an owner's decision or external circumstance rather than tenant misconduct.

LAHD identifies qualifying situations that may include an owner or immediate family member moving into the property, a required resident manager move-in, demolition, permanent removal of the unit from the rental market, conversion to non-residential use and certain government orders.

Those situations may trigger relocation-assistance obligations. An apparently straightforward plan like wanting to move into a rental can have notice, eligibility, relocation and procedural requirements.

What if I own a single-family house?

A single-family rental inside the City of Los Angeles should not automatically be assumed exempt. LAHD specifically notes that JCO can apply to a property containing only one single-family dwelling.

That surprises some owners because they associate Los Angeles landlord regulation with apartment buildings constructed before 1978. The JCO reaches a different category of housing.

State AB 1482 exemptions for certain single-family homes are separate questions, and those exemptions can depend on ownership structure and required tenant notices.

What about duplexes?

Duplexes require particularly careful analysis because owner occupancy, property configuration, RSO status and state law can all matter.

This is another reason I would not tell a buyer that it is only two units, so the tenant rules are simple. Two physically similar duplexes can have very different regulatory situations depending on construction date, tenancy, occupancy and jurisdiction.

For an investor, regulation is part of property due diligence.

Do JCO properties have to be registered?

LAHD says rental properties must be registered annually, and landlords must complete the applicable Rent Registry requirements.

Once registration is completed, the registration certificate must be displayed conspicuously at the property or served to the tenant. That is an operational responsibility that buyers should understand before closing on a rental.

What notices do Los Angeles landlords need to provide?

LAHD's current JCO guidance identifies multiple notice obligations.

Beginning August 20, 2025, landlords must post a Notice of Right to Counsel in a conspicuous common area, provide it at the beginning of a tenancy, and provide it when an eviction notice is served.

Residential landlords must also provide the City's Notice of Renters' Protections to qualifying new or renewing tenants and post it in an accessible common area. For an investor buying occupied property, those administrative requirements belong on the due-diligence checklist.

Do eviction notices have to be filed with the City?

Yes. LAHD says eviction notices issued for JCO and RSO rental properties must be filed with the department within three business days after service on the tenant.

That is exactly the kind of requirement that can be missed when an owner treats a tenancy as a private arrangement rather than a regulated business relationship.

What should buyers investigate before purchasing an occupied rental?

I would want a buyer to understand which units are occupied, what the current rents are, when each tenancy began, whether written leases are available, which local and state rules apply, whether the property has been properly registered, whether there are unresolved housing-code issues, whether required notices have been provided, whether there are disputes or delinquent rent, and whether the investment plan depends on a tenant vacating.

That final question matters a lot. If the entire financial plan requires immediately recovering possession of an occupied unit, the buyer should understand whether that assumption is actually realistic before removing contingencies.

Why this matters when valuing a rental property

A tenant is not just a line on a rent roll. The terms and legal status of that tenancy can affect income, timing, renovations, financing, owner occupancy and future strategy.

Imagine two identical duplexes. One has a vacant unit. The other has a long-term occupied unit subject to applicable tenant protections. Those properties may offer very different options to a buyer even if their physical condition is identical.

That is why tenant due diligence belongs beside inspection, title, insurance and financing.

Frequently asked questions

Does JCO apply only to old buildings? No. LAHD says JCO can apply to buildings newer than October 1, 1978.

Can JCO apply to a single-family rental? Yes. LAHD states that the ordinance can apply to a property containing only one single-family dwelling.

Is JCO the same as rent control? No. JCO itself does not regulate rent increases. Other city or state laws may separately regulate rent depending on the property.

Can an owner move into a JCO property? Owner or qualifying family occupancy can be a recognized no-fault reason in certain situations, but procedural and relocation requirements may apply. Owners should obtain legal advice before serving notices.

Do Los Angeles landlords have to file eviction notices with LAHD? LAHD says eviction notices for JCO and RSO properties must be filed within three business days of service.

Paul's take

One of the most dangerous assumptions an investor can make in Los Angeles is that a property is simple because it is not RSO.

The better question is: What rules actually apply to this property and these tenancies?

That answer can materially affect the economics of a purchase. Before buying an occupied duplex, fourplex, house or apartment building, I want the rent roll, leases, tenancy history and regulatory status looked at together rather than separately.

This article is general real-estate information, not legal advice. Owners dealing with an eviction or interpreting a specific exemption should consult an attorney familiar with Los Angeles landlord-tenant law.
